items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The way words (such as a caption) fix the meaning of an image that could otherwise be read in several ways"?
items.answer: anchorage

items.stem: Distinguish between a long shot and a close-up.
items.answer: A close-up fills the frame with the subject's face or a detail, creating intimacy and emotion; a long shot shows the subject in their setting, giving context and distance.
items.markingKey: A close-up fills the frame with the subject's face or a detail, creating intimacy and emotion; a long shot shows the subject in their setting, giving context and distance. items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a language-learning app, published in an in-flight magazine.

[Image: a grandmother and a teenage boy laugh across a kitchen table in Lisbon; steam rises from two cups.]
She never learned English. He never learned Portuguese. Until now.
Fifteen minutes a day. That's all it takes to turn 'Olá' into a conversation.
Lingo Bridge – because some words can't wait for a translator.
Download free. First month on us.

Explain why the visual composition of this text suits its purpose.
items.answer: The warm kitchen, rising steam and shared laughter connote intimacy; placing the two generations face to face across the table visually enacts the "bridge" of the brand name.
items.markingKey: The warm kitchen, rising steam and shared laughter connote intimacy; placing the two generations face to face across the table visually enacts the "bridge" of the brand name. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Ana writes: "Visual analysis is just describing what is in the picture." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Description is only the start; analysis explains how choices of composition, colour and framing create meaning and affect the viewer.
items.markingKey: Description is only the start; analysis explains how choices of composition, colour and framing create meaning and affect the viewer. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following homepage of a fictional university in Singapore, described in words.

[Banner photograph: four smiling students of different ethnicities walk across a sunlit lawn; one carries a robotic arm.]

Menu bar: Study | Research | Life on Campus | Apply Now – 'Apply Now' is an orange button, the only coloured item.
Scrolling ticker: 'Ranked #1 in Asia for graduate employability*'.
Pop-up chat window: 'Hi! I'm Ava, your student guide. What would you like to discover today?'

Explain how composition, colour or framing are used in this text and their effect.
items.answer: The diverse group walking forwards in sunlight connotes inclusion and progress; the robotic arm signals technological innovation; layout guides the eye from banner to orange button.
items.markingKey: The diverse group walking forwards in sunlight connotes inclusion and progress; the robotic arm signals technological innovation; layout guides the eye from banner to orange button. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). The Atlas X7. Built for the man who carries everyone.

items.answer: The father is framed centrally at the wheel with sleeping children behind him; dusk mountains connote adventure and trust; the tiny small print visually downplays fuel consumption.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "In a multimodal text the image always matters more than the words."
items.answer: Usually the image draws attention but words direct interpretation; their interplay matters most.

Arguments against: captions anchor meaning; slogans are often the most memorable element. Supported judgement: Usually the image draws attention but words direct interpretation; their interplay matters most.

items.answer: Indicative content: clear audience and purpose; justified visual choices with connotations; a slogan anchoring the image; evaluation of likely effect.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: clear audience and purpose; justified visual choices with connotations; a slogan anchoring the image; evaluation of likely effect.

items.stem: Explain why the relationship between image and text is important in multimodal texts.
items.answer: Words and images can reinforce, extend or contradict each other; their interplay creates meanings neither would produce alone.

[Image: a commuter's hand grips a matte-green bottle against a blurred, grey crowd.]
Every minute, a million plastic bottles are sold worldwide. You only need one.
FLOW. Steel-built. Leak-proof. Yours for life.
Fill it. Carry it. Keep it.
Refill free at 300 stations across the city – find yours on the FLOW app.

Guiding question: How does the advertisement persuade its audience that an individual purchase can address a global problem?
Write one analytical paragraph that answers the guiding question, using at least two references to the text.
items.answer: Thesis: the advertisement shrinks a global crisis to the scale of one commuter's routine. (1) The parallel headline links personal and planetary urgency. (2) The statistic set against "You only need one" turns guilt into empowerment. (3) The imperative tricolon and the green-against-grey image make the purchase simple and morally distinctive. Evaluation: the text arguably commodifies environmentalism – it solves over-consumption by selling another product (greenwashing).

Read the following three-panel comic strip, described in words.

[Panel 1: a world leader at a podium declares, 'We pledge to reach net zero by 2050!' Applause lines fill the background.]
[Panel 2: a polar bear on a shrinking ice floe raises a paw: 'Question – what's the plan for this summer?']

items.answer: To satirise long-term climate pledges that avoid immediate action. Supporting feature: "a polar bear on a shrinking ice floe raises a paw" (anthropomorphism) – the bear behaves like a journalist, giving the affected environment a voice.

Read the following home-front poster from a fictional wartime nation, written in the style of 1940s propaganda.

[Image: a woman in overalls rolls up her sleeve beside a factory gate; behind her, the silhouettes of marching soldiers.]
THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT.
YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE.
Every shell you make is a letter home.
Don't let them down – report for factory work today.

Which stylistic feature is used in "THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT. YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE."?
items.answer: parallelism
items.markingKey: D. "THEIR COURAGE AT THE FRONT. YOUR STRENGTH AT THE LATHE." is an example of parallelism: the matching structure makes factory work equal to fighting and binds the reader to the soldiers.

items.stem: Explain the role of timing in a three-panel comic strip.
items.answer: The panels act like beats in a joke – set-up, development, punchline – so the gutter between panels creates anticipation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The panels act like beats in a joke – set-up, development, punchline – so the gutter between panels creates anticipation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a static web page and an interactive interface.
items.answer: A static page presents fixed content to be read; an interactive interface responds to the user's actions (buttons, chat, forms), shaping their path and choices.
items.markingKey: A static page presents fixed content to be read; an interactive interface responds to the user's actions (buttons, chat, forms), shaping their path and choices. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a "demand" image and an "offer" image.
items.answer: In a demand image the subject looks at the viewer, requiring a response; in an offer image the subject looks away and is presented for the viewer to contemplate.
items.markingKey: In a demand image the subject looks at the viewer, requiring a response; in an offer image the subject looks away and is presented for the viewer to contemplate. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a language-learning app, published in an in-flight magazine.

[Image: a grandmother and a teenage boy laugh across a kitchen table in Lisbon; steam rises from two cups.]
She never learned English. He never learned Portuguese. Until now.
Fifteen minutes a day. That's all it takes to turn 'Olá' into a conversation.
Lingo Bridge – because some words can't wait for a translator.
Download free. First month on us.

Explain how the emotive language "some words can't wait for a translator" helps to sell the product.
items.answer: Emotive language: "some words can't wait for a translator" – it implies that family love is urgent and cannot be mediated, raising the emotional stakes of the purchase.
items.markingKey: Emotive language: "some words can't wait for a translator" – it implies that family love is urgent and cannot be mediated, raising the emotional stakes of the purchase. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an infographic and a cartoon.
items.answer: An infographic aims to inform through data presented visually and claims objectivity; a cartoon comments on events through exaggeration and humour, openly expressing a viewpoint.
items.markingKey: An infographic aims to inform through data presented visually and claims objectivity; a cartoon comments on events through exaggeration and humour, openly expressing a viewpoint. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Aiko writes: "Websites are neutral containers for information." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Website design makes choices about salience, order and interaction that persuade users and construct an identity for the organisation.
items.markingKey: Website design makes choices about salience, order and interaction that persuade users and construct an identity for the organisation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Typography is decoration and does not affect meaning." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Typefaces carry connotations (a serif font suggests tradition, a hand-drawn one intimacy) and size creates hierarchy.
items.markingKey: Typefaces carry connotations (a serif font suggests tradition, a hand-drawn one intimacy) and size creates hierarchy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a family SUV, printed in a weekend newspaper magazine.

[Image: a father at the wheel, two children asleep in the back, mountains at dusk through the windscreen.]
HE'S GOT THIS.
Seven seats. Five-star safety. Zero doubts.
The Atlas X7. Built for the man who carries everyone.
[Small print: 7.9 L/100 km combined. Model shown with optional extras.]

Explain what the advertisement is really selling beyond the product itself.
items.answer: Desire is constructed around being the dependable father: the car is sold as proof of masculine competence and family safety.
items.markingKey: Desire is constructed around being the dependable father: the car is sold as proof of masculine competence and family safety. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following meme shared on a student forum, described in words.

[Image, top: a tiny kitten stares bravely at an enormous, overflowing laundry basket. Top text: 'ME IN SEPTEMBER: I'LL START MY IA EARLY THIS YEAR'.]
[Image, bottom: the same kitten, now buried under the laundry, only its ears showing. Bottom text: 'ME, 11:58 P.M. THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DEADLINE'.]

Explain how the visual design of this text makes its message quick to understand.
items.answer: The kitten's small size against the huge basket visualises being overwhelmed; capital Impact-style text is a meme convention.
items.markingKey: The kitten's small size against the huge basket visualises being overwhelmed; capital Impact-style text is a meme convention. Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following homepage of a fictional university in Singapore, described in words.

[Banner photograph: four smiling students of different ethnicities walk across a sunlit lawn; one carries a robotic arm.]
Headline: 'Shape What's Next.'
Menu bar: Study | Research | Life on Campus | Apply Now – 'Apply Now' is an orange button, the only coloured item.
Scrolling ticker: 'Ranked #1 in Asia for graduate employability*'.
Pop-up chat window: 'Hi! I'm Ava, your student guide. What would you like to discover today?'

Analyse the effect of the single orange "Apply Now" button in the text.
items.answer: The single orange "Apply Now" button: colour contrast directs the eye to the desired action.
items.markingKey: The single orange "Apply Now" button: colour contrast directs the eye to the desired action. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following description of Dorothea Lange's photograph 'Migrant Mother' (1936) with its original caption.

[A black-and-white photograph. A woman in worn clothes sits under a tent, her hand raised to her chin, her eyes looking past the camera with a worried expression. Two children lean on her shoulders, faces turned away; a baby lies in her lap. The frame is tight, cutting out the surroundings.]
Caption (US Farm Security Administration file): 'Destitute pea pickers in California. Mother of seven children. Age thirty-two. Nipomo, California.'

Discuss the relationship between image and words in this text.
items.answer: The hand at the chin, the triangular composition and the turned-away children concentrate emotion on the mother's face; black-and-white tones emphasise documentary seriousness.
items.markingKey: The hand at the chin, the triangular composition and the turned-away children concentrate emotion on the mother's face; black-and-white tones emphasise documentary seriousness. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Compare how two advertisements you have studied construct desire for their products.
items.answer: Indicative content: identify the desire constructed in each; analyse image, slogan, appeals; compare audiences; evaluate ethics.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: identify the desire constructed in each; analyse image, slogan, appeals; compare audiences; evaluate ethics.

items.stem:
Read the following three-panel comic strip, described in words.

[Panel 1: a world leader at a podium declares, 'We pledge to reach net zero by 2050!' Applause lines fill the background.]
[Panel 2: a polar bear on a shrinking ice floe raises a paw: 'Question – what's the plan for this summer?']
[Panel 3: the leader, sweating, looks away: 'Next question.']

Guiding question: How does the comic strip criticise political responses to climate change?
Write one analytical paragraph that answers the guiding question, using at least two references to the text.
items.answer: Thesis: the strip contrasts distant promises with present danger. (1) Pledge and applause as performance. (2) The bear as questioner. (3) Evasion as punchline. Evaluation: effective simplification, though it treats all pledges as empty.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Thesis: the strip contrasts distant promises with present danger. (1) Pledge and applause as performance. (2) The bear as questioner. (3) Evasion as punchline. Evaluation: effective simplification, though it treats all pledges as empty. Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.
